items.question: A team is weighing a move from a higher-capability tier to a cheaper one for a production step. Which evidence should carry the most weight in that decision?

options.A: The measured cost difference per request between the two tiers, projected over current monthly volume.
options.B: Published benchmark comparisons between the two tiers on general reasoning and instruction-following suites.
options.C: A held-out eval set sampled from this step's production traffic, scored on the metric the step is accountable for.
options.D: A side-by-side review of a dozen hand-picked examples by the engineer who wrote and tuned the prompt.

items.question: A grocery retailer runs a two-step returns pipeline. Step 1 classifies an incoming free-text return request into one of nine dispositions; step 2 drafts a customer-facing response that quotes policy. Both run on Opus today. Step 1 sees 100% of traffic; step 2 runs on the 30% that are not auto-approved. The current eval shows step 1 at 98% agreement with human labels and step 2 at 81%, against the 90% the CX director signed off on. A keyword rules engine was trialled for step 1 two years ago and topped out at 74%. API spend is the team's second-largest line item. What is the best change?

options.A: Move both steps to a single cheaper tier so the team maintains one prompt library, one tier and one eval harness.
options.B: Keep both steps on the current tier and enable extended thinking on step 1 to push classification agreement higher.
options.C: Move step 1 to Haiku behind its own eval gate, and leave step 2 on the higher tier while its shortfall is worked separately.
options.D: Reinstate the 74% keyword rules engine for step 1 and redirect the entire API saving into a rewrite of the step 2 policy prompt.

items.question: A telco's voice IVR calls a model once per caller turn. The team's SLO is 1.2s p95 for that call, because anything slower produces dead air the caller reacts to. To fix a class of multi-step billing questions — about 6% of turns — the team enabled extended thinking on the step. Agreement on those questions rose from 62% to 88%, but measured p95 across all turns went from 0.9s to 4.7s and caller drop-off in the first minute rose. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep extended thinking on and reduce the reasoning budget until the measured p95 fits inside the 1.2s SLO.
options.B: Raise the SLO for the model call to 5s and communicate the change, since the accuracy gain on billing questions justifies the wait.
options.C: Move the step to the highest capability tier without extended thinking, on the basis that a stronger model reaches the same answer without an explicit reasoning pass.
options.D: Remove extended thinking from the synchronous turn and route the multi-step billing intents into an asynchronous flow that can afford the reasoning time.

items.question: For which kind of step is an extended-thinking budget most likely to repay its added latency and token cost?

options.A: High-volume extraction of fixed fields from a well-formed, unchanging template.
options.B: Single-turn classification into a small, mutually exclusive set of labels.
options.C: A planning step that must reconcile several interacting constraints before it commits.
options.D: Rewriting supplied text so that it conforms to a house style guide.

items.question: A motor insurer adjudicates 200,000 low-value claims a month. Today every claim goes to Opus. A proposed cascade runs Haiku on all claims first, with a confidence detector escalating uncertain cases to Opus. Measurement on a labelled sample: Haiku alone reaches the accepted standard on 70% of claims; the detector flags 45% of traffic for escalation and catches 96% of the claims Haiku got wrong. Compliance has agreed a ceiling of 0.5% of claims being wrongly adjudicated without escalation. What should the architect conclude?

options.A: Ship the cascade: it removes 55% of the higher-tier volume, and the residual error sits inside the variance the team already tolerates between eval runs.
options.B: Abandon the cascade and keep every claim on the higher tier, because a router that is not perfect can never satisfy a compliance ceiling.
options.C: Tighten the detector until fewer than one in sixty of Haiku's errors escape, then re-measure the saving at the escalation rate that requires.
options.D: Replace the confidence detector with extended thinking on the Haiku step so it self-corrects before the escalation decision is taken.

items.question: A logistics operator processes about 12,000 proof-of-delivery photos a day. Each photo shows a printed waybill number, a handwritten signature block, and sometimes visible damage to the parcel. An existing OCR service already feeds a text-only model. The team is deciding whether to send the photos to a vision-capable model directly instead. Which TWO considerations should drive the decision? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Sending the photo directly preserves layout, handwriting and parcel-condition cues that a flat OCR text dump discards, including the damage field OCR cannot populate.
options.B: Image input consumes tokens in proportion to the image, so a per-photo token budget has to be modelled before the design can be costed at this daily volume.
options.C: A vision-capable model removes the need to evaluate the extraction step, because the model reads the image the way a human reviewer would.
options.D: OCR followed by a text-only model is cheaper per document than image input in every case, so the comparison reduces to whether accuracy is acceptable.
options.E: Sending the image directly makes the extracted waybill number deterministic across repeated runs, unlike an OCR-plus-model chain where two stages each vary independently.

items.question: A market-research publisher generates a quarterly sector report of roughly 40 pages across 11 sections. The pipeline sends the outline, the quarter's data tables and the house style guide in one request and asks for the whole report. Responses consistently come back with a max-tokens stop reason partway through section 4, and an editor has to stitch the rest by hand. Inputs occupy a small fraction of the context window. What is the right design change?

options.A: Keep the single call but move the job to the highest capability tier, on the assumption a stronger model expresses the same content in fewer tokens.
options.B: Add an instruction capping every section at roughly 150 words, so the finished 11-section report fits inside a single response.
options.C: Generate section by section, passing the shared outline and summaries of prior sections into each call, and assemble in application code.
options.D: Retry the truncated call at temperature 1.0 so the model varies its structure and reaches the eleventh section before it stops.

items.question: In a design review, an engineer asks why a 60,000-token contract can be sent in one request but a full rewrite of it cannot be returned in one response. What is the accurate explanation?

options.A: Input tokens consume the response allowance one for one, so a 60,000-token input arithmetically leaves nothing for the model to answer with once the prompt is accounted for.
options.B: Rewriting requires the model to attend to the whole document simultaneously, and that kind of whole-document attention is not supported beyond a span of a few thousand tokens.
options.C: The response limit is a per-account throttle protecting shared capacity, and support can raise it once an account demonstrates a sustained need over a billing period.
options.D: Context window capacity and maximum single-response length are separate limits; a request can sit well inside the window and still be capped far below the room left.

items.question: A pharmacovigilance team codes adverse-event narratives to a controlled vocabulary. A newer, higher-capability tier scores clearly better on published reasoning benchmarks. The team ran its own blind eval on 600 labelled narratives: agreement is 91.4% on the current tier and 91.7% on the new one, with overlapping confidence intervals. Slice analysis shows the new tier fixes 6 of the current tier's 52 failures and introduces 5 new ones. Measured cost per case is 3.1x and p95 latency 2.4x. The programme director wants to upgrade 'to stay current'. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Discard the internal eval on the grounds that 600 narratives cannot resolve a gap that a benchmark of tens of thousands of items detected, and follow the benchmark.
options.B: Upgrade, because benchmark gains generally transfer to production tasks once the prompt has been retuned and the few-shot examples refreshed for the newer tier.
options.C: Stay on the current tier, log the eval as the decision record, and re-test when the failure profile, the vocabulary or the eval set changes.
options.D: Upgrade only the cases the current tier gets wrong, routed by a confidence signal, so the higher tier is paid for on 8.6% of volume.

items.question: A public-sector agency uses Claude to draft the written reasoning attached to benefits eligibility decisions. The decisions are appealable for six years, and on appeal the tribunal may ask how a particular explanation was produced. The service currently calls a floating model alias and stores only the final letter. What change most directly meets the obligation?

options.A: Set temperature to zero so the same case inputs always regenerate the same explanation.
options.B: Keep the floating alias but archive the final letter in immutable storage, since the letter is the artefact under appeal.
options.C: Snapshot the prompt template in version control and rely on the provider's deprecation notice period to keep model behaviour stable across the retention period.
options.D: Pin each request to a specific model version and record that exact version identifier with the prompt, inputs and response in the case record.

items.question: An energy utility drafts customer outage communications with Claude, pinned to a specific model version. The provider has issued a deprecation notice with a retirement date about five months out. The service uses 14 prompts, three of them heavily tuned with hand-selected few-shot examples. There is no eval set; quality has been judged by the content lead spot-checking a sample each week. The migration is now on the roadmap. What should the team do first?

options.A: Rewrite the three heavily tuned prompts to remove their few-shot examples, since hand-selected examples are the main source of version sensitivity.
options.B: Request an extension to the retirement date and defer the migration work until the extension is refused.
options.C: Build a regression eval set from logged production traffic, labelled against current behaviour, so the migration has a measurable baseline.
options.D: Point staging at the successor version and have the on-call engineer spot-check a day of traffic to see whether anything obvious breaks.

items.question: A manufacturer uses Claude to propose a root cause for line-stoppage tickets before a reliability engineer reviews it. The team swept the reasoning budget on a 400-ticket eval: at the smallest setting agreement with the engineers' eventual finding was 74%, at medium 88%, at large 89.5%, and at the largest 89.4%. Measured latency rises roughly linearly with the budget, and token cost rises with the reasoning produced. The agreed target is 88%. Which setting should go to production?

options.A: Turn extended thinking off and move up a tier instead; 74% at the smallest setting shows the model is underpowered for this task.
options.B: Take the largest setting in the sweep, since more reasoning headroom is strictly safer for a step where a missed root cause keeps a line stopped.
options.C: Take the large setting and treat its margin over the medium setting as the buffer the 88% target implies.
options.D: Take the medium setting, and re-run the sweep when the ticket mix or the prompt changes.

items.question: Pinning a production request to a specific model version primarily protects against which risk?

options.A: Requests-per-minute and token-per-minute quotas on the account being revised by the provider.
options.B: Behaviour drift caused by the team's own unreviewed edits to its prompt templates.
options.C: Run-to-run variation between two identical requests sent moments apart to the same pinned model version.
options.D: System behaviour changing without a deployment because the provider's default target moved.

items.question: A container shipping line is reviewing candidate steps in its stowage-planning system for an extended-thinking budget. Which THREE conditions, if true of a step, argue in favour of spending reasoning budget on it? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The step's failures are predominantly cases where the model committed to an answer before reconciling all the stated constraints.
options.B: The step runs off the synchronous user path, so extra seconds per call are absorbed by a queue rather than seen by a user.
options.C: The step's failures are predominantly cases where the fact needed to answer was never present in the context supplied.
options.D: An eval sweep shows accuracy rising materially as the reasoning budget grows, before flattening at a measurable point.
options.E: The step already runs on the highest capability tier, so reasoning budget is the only remaining lever available.

items.question: A crop insurer receives about 9,000 field photographs a week from policyholders. Stage 1 decides whether a photo is usable and whether it shows crop damage at all; roughly 40% pass. Stage 2 assigns a severity band, which determines the payment. Today a single Opus call with the image does both, and the image cost dominates the per-photo bill. An eval shows stage 1 at 97% agreement and stage 2 at 92%, both above target. What is the best change?

options.A: Downscale every image before sending so the per-photo token cost falls, keeping the single combined call.
options.B: Keep the single call and add extended thinking, so the severity band comes with a stronger justification for the adjuster.
options.C: Run the usability-and-damage screen on a cheaper tier and send only the photos that pass to the higher tier for severity banding.
options.D: Move both stages to the cheaper tier and add human review of every assigned severity band before payment is released.

items.question: A litigation team is building a question-answering tool over a discovery set of about 2.3 million pages. A developer proposes putting the case file into the context window so the model can 'see everything'. What should the architect do?

options.A: Load the corpus into the context window and rely on the model's long-context recall to find the relevant passages.
options.B: Split the corpus across parallel calls, one document per call, and have a final call merge every per-document answer.
options.C: Defer the feature until a model with a context window large enough for the whole corpus becomes available.
options.D: Retrieve a small, relevant subset per question and spend the window budget on that evidence plus the instructions.

items.question: An online games publisher re-scores 4.1 million player-report summaries every night and must finish inside a 6-hour maintenance window. The job runs on a mid tier; at the account's concurrency ceiling the current run takes 9.5 hours and has started overrunning into peak hours. Traffic analysis shows 82% of reports are single-category and unambiguous. The moderation lead will not accept a measurable quality regression. Which TWO changes most directly bring the job inside the window? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Route the 82% of single-category, unambiguous reports to a faster, cheaper tier and keep the remainder on the current tier, after an eval confirms no regression on the split.
options.B: Have the model emit only the fields that changed rather than restating the full record, cutting generated tokens per report.
options.C: Move the whole job to the highest capability tier, on the basis that a stronger model needs fewer retries and so finishes sooner.
options.D: Enable extended thinking so fewer reports require a second pass through the pipeline.
options.E: Raise the sampling temperature so the model commits to an answer sooner and spends less time generating.

items.question: A home-goods retailer extracts structured product attributes from supplier catalogues. Overnight, schema-conformance of the model's JSON output fell from 99.6% to 94.1% and has stayed there. There was no deploy that day, no change to the supplier feed, and no infrastructure event. The service calls a floating model alias. The downstream catalogue ingest rejects non-conforming records, and a backlog is building. What should the team do next?

options.A: Add a repair step downstream that fixes malformed JSON before ingest, and continue on the current floating alias.
options.B: Rewrite the prompt with more explicit schema instructions and redeploy, since output-format failures are usually prompt problems.
options.C: Raise a vendor support ticket and pause the feature until a response is received from the provider.
options.D: Pin the request to the version serving before the change, confirm conformance recovers, then evaluate the newer version behind a flag.

items.question: Which finding most justifies moving a production step up to a higher capability tier?

options.A: Cost per request has fallen enough elsewhere in the programme that the budget can comfortably absorb the higher tier at current volume.
options.B: A newer and more capable tier has become generally available, and the team is still on the one chosen at inception.
options.C: Residual errors are concentrated in cases needing multi-step inference, and further prompt and context work has stopped moving the metric.
options.D: Stakeholders reviewing sample outputs in a demo have asked for responses that sound more authoritative and less hedged.

items.question: An investor-relations analytics firm extracts around 60 KPIs per annual report. Roughly 30% of them appear only inside charts and infographics — never in the narrative text or the tabular financial statements. The current pipeline runs a text extraction service and then a text-only model; those KPIs come back either null or with a plausible-looking value inferred from the prose near the figure, which is worse. What is the right change?

options.A: Render the figure-bearing pages as images for a vision-capable model, keeping the existing text path for narrative and tables.
options.B: Widen the text extracted around each figure caption so the model has more surrounding prose to work from when inferring the value.
options.C: Move the text pipeline to the highest tier so it reasons more carefully about the prose and captions around each figure.
options.D: Have the model mark chart-derived KPIs as unavailable and route all 18 of them per report to an analyst for manual entry.

items.question: An education provider grades free-text exam answers with a model-based grader whose score drives a pass/fail outcome. The grader and the answer-feedback generator both run on the same mid tier, chosen for cost. An audit against two expert human raters puts grader-to-expert agreement at 79%; the accreditation body requires 92%. The generator's feedback quality is not under complaint. An engineer proposes moving the generator to the highest tier. What should the architect do?

options.A: Move the generator to the higher tier, on the basis that better-written answers and feedback are easier to grade consistently.
options.B: Keep both on the current tier and average three independent grader calls per answer so scoring variance against the rubric falls.
options.C: Move the grader to the higher tier and re-measure agreement against the expert-rated set before changing anything about the generator.
options.D: Replace the grader with exact-match scoring of each answer against a model reference answer held in the question bank.

items.question: A published leaderboard shows one tier clearly outperforming another on a coding benchmark. What may an architect legitimately conclude for a document-classification service?

options.A: That the stronger tier will classify documents more accurately, because coding ability correlates with general reasoning.
options.B: That the stronger tier will need fewer few-shot examples to reach the same classification accuracy.
options.C: Nothing at all, since results on one benchmark are not comparable across tiers.
options.D: Only that the tier is worth shortlisting for an eval on the classification task; the benchmark itself says nothing more.

items.question: A national rail operator summarises safety incident reports for a weekly review board. The step runs on a mid tier and sits four points below the agreed accuracy target. The team is considering an upgrade. Which TWO findings would genuinely support that decision? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Residual failures concentrate on reports where the model must reconcile contradictory witness statements, and three rounds of prompt and context revision have not moved the metric.
options.B: A pilot on the higher tier resolves a material share of those residual failures, at a cost per report the programme has budget for.
options.C: The current tier's model version carries a deprecation notice with a retirement date next year, so the step has to be moved to a different version before then.
options.D: Measured p95 latency on the current tier is already above the team's own service objective for the weekly summarisation step.
options.E: The residual failures are cases where the incident report referenced a witness appendix that the pipeline never retrieved.

items.question: A national library runs two Claude workloads. One is an interactive search summariser for researchers, with a 2s p95 objective. The other is an overnight metadata enrichment job across 6 million scanned items, with the whole night available. Both currently run on the same tier, chosen 'for consistency'. Which TWO statements correctly explain why the tier decision should be made separately for each? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Using one tier across both workloads is required once they share a prompt template, because a template is bound to the tier it was authored against.
options.B: Interactive workloads should use the cheapest available tier, because users value responsiveness over accuracy and the 2s p95 objective is the only binding constraint.
options.C: The overnight job's binding constraint is cost per acceptable result across 6 million items, while the interactive path's tier is bounded by what fits inside 2s p95.
options.D: The overnight job should use the cheapest tier by definition, since work with no user waiting on it carries no quality requirement to defend.
options.E: With no user waiting, the overnight job can afford a higher tier or a reasoning budget if the eval shows better metadata quality.

items.question: A hospital group drafts discharge summaries with Claude; a clinician reviews and signs every one. To cut cost the team evaluated a cheaper tier offline on 500 historical cases: rubric agreement is within one point of the current tier and measured cost per summary falls by about two thirds. The clinical safety officer owns the sign-off and has previously rejected changes evidenced only by aggregate scores. What should the team do next?

options.A: Roll out to all wards at once and watch the clinician edit-rate dashboard for a week, rolling back if the rate rises above its current baseline.
options.B: Ask the clinical safety officer to sign off on the offline eval alone, on the grounds that 500 cases is a statistically adequate sample for a one-point difference.
options.C: Roll out on a single ward first and let the clinicians there raise problems informally through their usual channels.
options.D: Shadow the cheaper tier on live traffic, score both outputs on the same clinical rubric, and take the paired comparison to the safety officer before any traffic moves.

items.question: A team is switching a failing text-extraction step to native image input. Which failure will image input NOT address?

options.A: Values that appear only inside a chart and never in the document's text.
options.B: Fields whose meaning depends on their position in a printed form's layout.
options.C: Fields that are genuinely absent from the document the user uploaded.
options.D: Handwritten annotations that the OCR service renders as noise.

items.question: A mortgage servicer processes borrower hardship packets containing bank statements, pay stubs and handwritten letters. A text-extraction service flattens each packet into one text blob before the model sees it. The dominant error is figures being attributed to the wrong column of a multi-column statement. The team already reconciles column totals where the statement prints them, which catches about a third of these misattributions. What is the right change?

options.A: Send the page images to a vision-capable model so column structure and table boundaries survive into the model's input.
options.B: Add an explicit instruction that each figure belongs to the column it is printed under, with two worked examples.
options.C: Move the extraction step to a higher tier so the model reasons more carefully about the flattened text.
options.D: Extend the reconciliation check to infer expected totals where the statement does not print them, so more misattributions are caught.

items.question: A university runs a research assistant over a policy corpus. Its eval reports faithfulness at 98% — nearly every statement is traceable to the context supplied — but answer completeness at only 61%. Error analysis of the incomplete answers shows that in 34% the required passage was never retrieved, and in a further 41% it was retrieved but ranked below the cut-off passed to the model. The team has proposed moving to the highest tier. What should the architect advise?

options.A: Upgrade the tier; a stronger model composes more complete answers from the same retrieved context.
options.B: Enable extended thinking so the model reasons harder about the context it does have.
options.C: Leave the tier alone and fix retrieval, because three quarters of the incomplete answers trace to a passage the model was never shown.
options.D: Increase the number of passages passed to the model until the context window is full, so the cut-off stops excluding relevant material.

items.question: An automotive supplier assigns causal codes to warranty claims. The step runs on Sonnet and scores 84% against a 90% target agreed with the quality organisation. Two proposals are on the table: move to Opus, or enable extended thinking on the current tier. The team is arguing the merits in the abstract and the decision has been open for three weeks. What should the architect do?

options.A: Move to Opus, because tier is the stronger lever and a reasoning budget can always be layered on afterwards if the target is still missed.
options.B: Run the two proposals as arms of one eval on the same held-out set, comparing accuracy gain against measured cost and p95 latency.
options.C: Enable extended thinking first, because a reasoning budget is a smaller change to make and therefore the cheaper of the two options.
options.D: Apply both changes together so the 90% target is cleared in a single release ahead of the quality organisation's next review.

items.question: How should an architect treat the reasoning tokens produced under an extended-thinking budget when sizing and costing a request?

options.A: As free, since the reasoning is internal working and is not the answer returned to the user.
options.B: As generated tokens that are paid for and that consume part of the response allowance.
options.C: As input tokens, since they are derived from the prompt that was supplied.
options.D: As tokens that count only when the caller chooses to have the reasoning surfaced.

items.question: A coroner's service is building a case-preparation assistant. A single inquest bundle — witness statements, medical records, expert reports and prior correspondence — can reach roughly 900,000 tokens, far beyond the context window, and the assistant must answer specific questions about the bundle with references. Which THREE are appropriate design responses to that constraint? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Retrieve per question and place only the passages relevant to that question in the window, with citations back to the source documents.
options.B: Raise the request's maximum response length so the model has more room to hold the bundle while it works.
options.C: Map over the bundle in sections with a per-section extraction step, then reduce the section outputs in a final call sized to fit the window.
options.D: Concatenate the whole bundle and rely on the oldest material being trimmed away, since the most recent documents are the most relevant to an inquest.
options.E: Carry a compact, application-maintained case digest forward between calls instead of the raw bundle, so each request's window holds a bounded amount.

items.question: A tour operator is migrating its itinerary-drafting service from a retiring model version to its successor. On the team's regression suite, 11 of the 14 prompts pass unchanged. The three that regress — from 93% to 78% — are the ones with hand-selected few-shot examples and detailed formatting cues accumulated over two years of tuning against the retiring version. Retirement is four months away. What is the right conclusion and response?

options.A: The successor is materially less capable on this task; escalate to the vendor, ask for the retirement date to be reversed, and pause the migration.
options.B: Reduce the temperature on the three affected prompts until the regression suite passes again, then re-baseline.
options.C: Keep the three affected prompts pinned to the retiring version until close to its retirement date, then revisit the problem.
options.D: The examples and formatting cues were tuned to the retiring version; re-select the examples and re-tune those three prompts on the same suite.

items.question: A six-person charity operations team wants a tool that drafts first-pass thank-you notes to donors. Every note is read and edited by a staff member before it is sent, volume is around 400 a week, and there is no capacity to build or maintain an eval programme. What tier posture should the architect recommend?

options.A: Start on the cheapest tier a quick hands-on review finds acceptable, since a human edits every output before it is sent.
options.B: Start on the highest tier so quality is never the constraint, and downgrade later once an eval set has been built.
options.C: Build a labelled eval set of 500 historical donor notes before committing to any tier, prompt or review process.
options.D: Match the tier already used by the charity's other Claude workload, purely for operational consistency.

items.question: A food-delivery marketplace normalises restaurant menus into its own schema. On a 2,000-menu benchmark the cheaper tier costs a measured £0.04 per menu in API spend and produces a correct normalisation 71% of the time; failures go to an operations queue whose measured handling cost is £2.10 per menu. The higher tier costs four times as much per menu in API spend and is correct 94% of the time. The error rate is flat across menu length. The finance lead objects that the higher tier 'quadruples our model spend'. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Stay on the cheaper tier: its API cost per menu is a quarter of the alternative's, and the operations queue is a standing team cost rather than a per-menu one.
options.B: Move to the higher tier: at the measured rework cost, total cost per menu falls from about £0.65 to about £0.29 even though API spend rises.
options.C: Stay on the cheaper tier and add extended thinking to close the accuracy gap for less than a tier change would cost.
options.D: Split by menu complexity, sending only long menus to the higher tier and keeping short ones on the cheaper one.

items.question: A title insurer extracts a fixed set of fields from scanned property deed packets that typically run 40 to 90 pages. The team plans to send the pages as images to a vision-capable model. Which TWO constraints most directly shape the design? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Sending pages as images removes the need for a page-ordering step, because the model infers document order from the content of each page.
options.B: Page images consume tokens in proportion to their size, so a 90-page packet's image footprint has to be budgeted against the context window.
options.C: Maximum response length grows with the number of input pages, so a 90-page packet can return a proportionally longer extraction than a 40-page one.
options.D: Only a few pages in a typical packet carry the fields being extracted, so a cheap page-selection pass ahead of extraction changes cost and window budget.
options.E: Scanned image input does not count against the context window, because it is handled by a separate vision path before the text model sees it.

items.question: A streaming service applies content advisory tags with Claude, pinned to a specific model version that has no deprecation notice. A newer version is now available. The team has a maintained regression suite and three months of logged production traffic. The product director wants to be on 'the newest model'; the trust-and-safety lead owns the advisory taxonomy and has not been consulted. What should the team do next?

options.A: Replay a stratified sample of logged traffic through both versions, compare on the regression suite and the sensitive slices, and hand the result to the trust-and-safety lead.
options.B: Move the pin to the newer version behind a kill switch, watch the tagging dashboards for a week, and revert if the tag distribution shifts.
options.C: Leave the pin where it is: with no deprecation pressure there is no reason to spend engineering effort evaluating a newer version until the provider forces the question.
options.D: Ask the vendor for a written summary of the behavioural differences between the two versions and make the adoption decision from that.

items.question: A shared internal client library enables extended thinking by default for every service that uses it. For which condition should a team explicitly disable it on one of their steps?

options.A: The step is on a latency-sensitive path and its eval shows no accuracy gain from the reasoning budget.
options.B: The step's outputs are reviewed by a named human approver before they are used downstream.
options.C: The step already runs on the highest capability tier, which the team chose for this workload at launch.
options.D: The step's prompt already asks the model to work through its reasoning step by step before answering.

items.question: A SaaS company runs release QA with an agent that drives a browser and asserts on the DOM. Last quarter 22% of escaped defects were visual — overlapping elements, clipped text, controls rendered in the wrong state — and every one of them passed the DOM assertions. Page content is data-driven and differs on each run. What is the right change?

options.A: Increase DOM assertion coverage to include the computed styles of every element on the page, covering position, overflow, z-index and visibility.
options.B: Screenshot each assertion point and have a vision-capable model check it against the expected visual description, alongside the DOM assertions.
options.C: Move the agent to a higher capability tier so it reasons more carefully about the DOM snapshot it is given at each assertion point.
options.D: Pixel-diff every screenshot against a stored baseline image and fail the run on any difference above a 0.5% per-page pixel tolerance.

items.question: A staffing firm parses about 300,000 CVs a month into structured profiles. Single-CV calls succeed on 99.3% of documents. To amortise a long system prompt, an engineer moved to 25 CVs per call. In the pilot, 18% of batches hit the response length ceiling and were lost entirely, and a single malformed CV corrupted the structured output for its whole batch. What should the team do?

options.A: Return to one CV per call; once responses are length-bounded and records share one structure, batching cannot be made safe at any useful size.
options.B: Keep 25 per batch and retry any truncated batch with an added instruction to be more concise about optional fields.
options.C: Cut the batch to a size whose worst-case output fits the response allowance, and emit one record per line so a malformed CV fails alone.
options.D: Keep 25 per batch and move to a higher capability tier, which will express the same records more compactly.

items.question: For a single request, what does the context window bound?

options.A: The size of the input only; the response is governed separately and does not draw on the window.
options.B: The combined size of the request's input and the response generated for it.
options.C: The total tokens the account may consume in a rolling time period.
options.D: The number of conversational turns before the exchange must be restarted.

items.question: A payments processor is migrating its dispute-narrative classifier from a pinned model version to its successor. The regression eval has passed on the successor, and the classifier's output feeds a decision that is disclosable to the card scheme. The cutover is scheduled for next week. Which TWO elements must the cutover plan include? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A commitment to remove the outgoing version's pin from the codebase on cutover day, to prevent configuration drift.
options.B: A recorded mapping of which model version served each request, so any decision taken during the cutover window can be attributed to a version.
options.C: A re-run of the regression eval against the outgoing pinned version to confirm it has not itself changed.
options.D: A rollback path that returns traffic to the outgoing version without requiring a code deploy.
options.E: A freeze on all prompt changes for the six months following cutover.

items.question: A county records office is digitising handwritten land registers spanning 1930 to 1975. A vendor demonstrated transcription on twelve clean pages and the results were impressive. The actual archive contains faded ink, heavy marginalia, water damage on some volumes, and typically two or three changes of clerk handwriting per volume. The programme has funding for one approach and cannot restart. What should the archivist's technical lead do first?

options.A: Proceed with the demo configuration and add a human verification pass on any page the model flags as low confidence, sampling the rest.
options.B: Pre-process every page with contrast enhancement and deskewing, then repeat the vendor demonstration.
options.C: Build an eval set stratified by decade, ink condition and clerk hand, and measure against transcribed ground truth before committing.
options.D: Commit to the highest capability tier now, since handwriting is the hardest visual task and capability is the deciding factor.

items.question: A public agency translates regulatory guidance into eleven languages. A typical source document is about 55,000 tokens. The pipeline sends the whole document and requests the full translation; responses truncate part-way through, and the published translations must be terminologically consistent with a mandated glossary. An engineer proposes moving to a model with a larger context window. What is the right response?

options.A: Adopt a model with a larger context window, since the 55,000-token source plus its translation together are what overflow.
options.B: Request a condensed translation that conveys the substance of each section within the available response length.
options.C: Detect truncation and issue a continuation request containing only an instruction to carry on from the cut, looping until the response completes.
options.D: Translate in segments against the mandated glossary, carrying the previous segment's tail forward, and assemble the document in code.

items.question: Twelve months after a model tier was chosen for a regulated workflow, an auditor asks the team to justify the choice. Which record set actually supports the justification?

options.A: The architecture diagram and the signed decision record naming the chosen tier and summarising the reasoning behind it.
options.B: The vendor's published capability comparison for the candidate tiers as it stood on the date the decision was taken, retained as a PDF.
options.C: Production monitoring dashboards covering the month following the decision, including error rate, latency and cost per case.
options.D: The eval set with its labelling provenance, the measured result for each candidate tier, and the pinned versions those results came from.

items.question: A field-service company runs an agent that plans an engineer's daily route and books the parts each job needs. A typical task takes 9 to 14 tool-calling turns. The team enabled extended thinking to improve planning quality. Task success rose from 76% to 88%, but mean cost per task rose 5.8x and p95 task duration went from 19s to 96s, against a dispatcher-facing target of 30s. Error analysis shows the improvement comes almost entirely from better initial routes, not from better individual bookings. What should the architect change?

options.A: Apply the reasoning budget only to the initial planning turn, run the tool-calling turns without it, and re-measure.
options.B: Keep the reasoning budget on all turns and move the whole agent to a cheaper tier to offset the cost increase.
options.C: Collapse the tool-calling turns into a single composite tool so the reasoning budget is paid far fewer times.
options.D: Keep the current configuration and raise the dispatcher-facing target from 30s to 100s to accommodate it.

items.question: A retail pharmacy chain pilots a cheaper tier for its medication-interaction summaries. Across the 12,000-case pilot, agreement moves from 94.1% to 93.8% — inside the eval's noise band. On the paediatric-dosing slice, 360 cases or 3% of volume, agreement falls from 96% to 87%. Two rounds of added paediatric examples in the prompt did not move that slice. What should the team do next?

options.A: Proceed with the full downgrade: the aggregate sits within noise and the affected slice is only 3% of volume.
options.B: Abandon the downgrade, since a nine-point regression on a clinical slice disqualifies the cheaper tier for this workflow entirely.
options.C: Route the paediatric-dosing slice to the higher tier and the rest to the cheaper one, if the slice can be identified before the call.
options.D: Re-run the pilot with a larger sample, since a 3% slice may not contain enough cases to measure a real difference.

items.question: A pipeline must read text and preserve reading order from born-digital PDFs that already contain a correct text layer. What is the most efficient input choice?

options.A: Render every page as an image and send it to a vision-capable model, so that nothing on the page can be missed by a faulty text extractor.
options.B: Pass the extracted text layer, which already carries the characters and their order, and reserve image input for pages where layout matters.
options.C: Send both the text layer and the page image for every page so the model can cross-check one representation against the other and flag mismatches.
options.D: Convert the PDF to a single plain-text blob and discard headings and table boundaries, since models handle unstructured text well enough.

items.question: A manufacturer photographs every weld on a production line and needs a model to classify each into one of five defect classes, at about 4,200 photographs per shift. The engineering lead has specified the highest capability tier on the reasoning that 'vision is hard'. A labelled set of 3,000 images with agreed defect-recall targets already exists. What should the architect do?

options.A: Use the highest tier for every photograph; defect classification affects product safety, and cost is secondary on a safety-critical line.
options.B: Use the cheapest tier and route low-confidence photographs to the highest tier, setting the confidence threshold before any tier has been measured.
options.C: Raise the capture resolution until the cheapest tier reaches the agreed recall bar, then lock the camera settings.
options.D: Run the existing labelled eval against each tier and take the cheapest that clears the agreed defect-recall bar on these images.

items.question: A media-monitoring company is deciding whether a sentiment-and-stance step has genuinely reached the ceiling of its current tier, or whether the remaining errors are a prompt or context problem that a cheaper fix would solve. Which THREE observations point to a capability ceiling? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Two engineers independently rewrote the step's instructions, and both results sit inside the eval's noise band.
options.B: Errors cluster on inputs where the source record arrived without the article body, leaving only a headline to judge.
options.C: Enlarging the supplied context so the model has strictly more relevant material produces no measurable improvement.
options.D: The step's p95 latency has risen steadily since launch as the average article length in the monitored feeds grew.
options.E: Human raters given exactly the model's input agree the correct answer is derivable from it, yet the model still gets it wrong.

items.question: At a payments company, engineers complain that strict version pinning stops them experimenting with newer models, while the operations team has been burned by unannounced behaviour changes and wants everything pinned. The team has a maintained regression suite that runs in staging. What pinning policy should the architect set?

options.A: Pin every environment, including local development, so behaviour is identical everywhere and no engineer debugs against a different model.
options.B: Let every environment float and rely on the CI regression suite to catch behavioural changes before they reach users, alerting on-call on failure.
options.C: Pin production and staging to the same version, let development and eval environments float, and promote only after the staging suite passes.
options.D: Pin production only and let staging float, so the team gets early warning of provider-side behaviour changes before they reach paying customers.

items.question: An airline is running a six-week phased migration: 20% of refund-eligibility explanations are generated by a new model version and 80% by the outgoing one, to gather comparative data. In week two, a customer disputes an explanation and the support team cannot determine which version produced it. Separately, the quality dashboard shows an overall dip that the team cannot attribute to either version. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Stamp the serving model version on every response record and surface it in the support tooling and the quality dashboard.
options.B: End the phased rollout and move all traffic onto one version so that attribution becomes unambiguous again.
options.C: Raise the new version's share to 50% so the dashboard's dip becomes large enough to detect statistically.
options.D: Record the serving version only for requests that later generate a complaint, to limit growth of the log store.

items.question: An audit firm ingests client trial balances and supporting schedules as PDFs. Roughly 60% are born-digital exports from accounting systems and the rest are scans of printed reports, some with handwritten annotations from the client's finance team. Which TWO statements should shape how the pipeline handles the two kinds? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Born-digital PDFs carry a text layer whose characters and order are already correct, so passing that text is cheaper and less error-prone than page images.
options.B: Whether a PDF is born-digital or scanned cannot be established programmatically, so the model must be asked to make that determination.
options.C: Scanned PDFs have no reliable text layer, so they need OCR or image input, and the choice turns on whether layout and handwritten marks carry meaning.
options.D: A single uniform path is preferable regardless, because handling two document classes doubles the number of failure modes the team must test.
options.E: Born-digital PDFs never contain graphics whose meaning would be lost in text extraction, so the text layer alone is sufficient for every accounting-system export.

items.question: A system moves from one model version to its successor within the same capability tier. What should the team expect to have to revisit?

options.A: Nothing, provided the tier is unchanged; successive versions within a tier are behaviour-compatible by design.
options.B: Prompt phrasing, few-shot example selection and output-format adherence, which can all shift between versions.
options.C: Only the model identifier string in configuration.
options.D: The retrieval index, which must be rebuilt whenever the generating model changes.

items.question: An event-ticketing company launches matchday support for a stadium in five weeks. The team's eval on the higher tier clears the agreed accuracy bar. The CFO has set a run-cost cap that the higher tier would exceed at projected matchday volume. The cheaper tier has never been evaluated. The product lead wants to ship on the cheaper tier to meet the cap. What should the team do next?

options.A: Run the existing eval against the cheaper tier this week, and take the measured quality gap and the cost of each option to the CFO.
options.B: Ship on the cheaper tier and monitor: the eval on the higher tier already proves the prompt works, and production monitoring will catch any shortfall.
options.C: Ship on the higher tier and ask the CFO to raise the cap after launch, once real volume data exists.
options.D: Build a cascade that starts on the cheaper tier and escalates on low confidence, so the cap is met without needing an eval.

items.question: A step that previously streamed its answer immediately is switched to use an extended-thinking budget. How does its latency profile change from the caller's point of view?

options.A: Time to the first answer token grows, because the model reasons before the answer begins.
options.B: Total latency is unchanged, because reasoning is produced in parallel with the answer tokens.
options.C: Time to the first answer token is unchanged, and only the total duration of the response grows.
options.D: Latency becomes constant across inputs, since the reasoning budget fixes the amount of work performed.

items.question: A water utility maintains around 9,000 device configuration documents averaging 30,000 tokens each. A regulatory change amends a clause that appears in every one of them. The current pipeline sends each document and asks for the full revised version: 40% of responses truncate, and engineers reviewing the change must diff a whole regenerated document against the original to see what actually moved. What is the right redesign?

options.A: Split each document at clause boundaries, request a full rewrite of each section, and concatenate the sections into one document.
options.B: Move to a higher capability tier so the full revised document, all 30,000 tokens of it, fits within the response allowance.
options.C: Have the model emit a structured list of targeted edits the application applies to the original, so response length scales with the change.
options.D: Pre-filter to the documents the amended clause actually touches and keep the existing full-rewrite approach for that subset.

items.question: A team reports that a candidate tier scored 100% on their 40-item smoke test. What may legitimately be concluded?

options.A: The tier is suitable for production on this task and the change can proceed to release.
options.B: Very little: a set this small with no failures gives almost no resolution on the true error rate.
options.C: The tier is at least as accurate as the incumbent, since the incumbent has never scored 100%.
options.D: The smoke test is too easy to be informative and should be replaced with a harder set.

items.question: A dating platform screens every outbound first message for harassment before it is delivered, at about 40 million messages a day. Product has allowed 150ms of p95 latency for the screen inside the send path. The screen currently runs on a mid tier and measures 480ms p95. Trust and safety will not accept a drop in recall on the categories that trigger account action. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep the mid tier in place and renegotiate the screening budget from 150ms to 500ms with the product team.
options.B: Move the screen off the send path and review messages after delivery instead.
options.C: Move the screen to the highest capability tier to maximise recall, on the basis that harassment screening is safety-critical.
options.D: Run the fastest tier inline against the 150ms budget and route only the borderline scoring band to the higher tier.

items.question: A regional newspaper group runs a five-step editorial pipeline on one tier. An engineer proposes splitting it across three tiers to cut cost. Which TWO conditions argue for keeping a single tier instead? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The pipeline's steps have visibly different difficulty profiles, with headline generation far simpler than the legal-risk read on each story.
options.B: The steps run sequentially rather than in parallel, with each step's output passed straight to the next as soon as it has been produced.
options.C: Each step would need separately tuned prompts and its own eval gate per tier, and one engineer maintains the whole pipeline.
options.D: The projected saving is small relative to total run cost, because the steps eligible for a cheaper tier are a minority of the tokens processed.
options.E: The pipeline already meets its accuracy and latency targets, with measured headroom against both on the current tier.

items.question: The same prompt is moved from a higher-capability tier to a cheaper one. Which prompt properties typically become load-bearing that were not before?

options.A: Explicitness of the required output format, and the number and quality of worked examples.
options.B: The politeness and register of the instructions.
options.C: Whether the prompt names the model tier it was written for.
options.D: The overall length of the system prompt, which must be shortened when moving to a cheaper tier.
